# Comedy, Gag Architecture and Escalation

Category `comedy`.

**Part 1 of 2.** 32 cards across the joke unit, timing, the engines that generate comedy, escalation and the long joke, the comic modes, comedy across formats and languages, and the named failure modes.

Comedy is engineering. It has load-bearing parts, a tolerance and a failure mode. A writer who says jokes "just come to them" is describing a machine they happen to run without looking at. This file looks at it.

## Section 1 — The Joke Unit

### Setup and Punchline

**Also called:** premise and payoff, the two-part joke, the bit
**What it is:** The setup builds an expectation in the audience's head; the punchline replaces it with a second, incompatible reading that was always available. The laugh is the sound of the switch.
**Effect on the audience:** A half-second of being wrong, then the pleasure of being wrong cheaply. Laughter is the discharge of an expectation that was loaded and then dumped.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every unit of written comedy sits on this except the observation whose accurate naming is itself the joke, which often has no punchline at all (`comedy.observational_truth`). The craft rule is that the setup must be the shortest true sentence that installs the wrong reading — every extra word is a chance for the audience to spot the second reading early. Load the setup with information, load the punchline with surprise, and never let them share a job.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, sketch, sitcom, prose, short-form video | genres: comedy, dramedy, satire, kids
**Avoid when:** The scene's job is dread or grief and you have no plan for what the laugh costs. A clean setup-punchline in the middle of a death scene does not leaven it, it cancels it — see `comedy.joke_that_stops_story`.
**Example:**
> My grandmother made it to ninety-four on cigarettes, lard and spite. The doctors called it a miracle.
>
> She called it a warm-up.

**Yields to:** `tens.comic_relief_as_tension` — where the scene's job is dread or grief. A clean setup-punchline in the middle of a death scene does not leaven it, it cancels it.  
`comedy.setup_punchline`

---

### The Rule of Three

**Also called:** the triple, the comic list, two-and-a-turn
**What it is:** Two items establish a pattern, the third breaks it. Three is the smallest number that can hold a pattern and a betrayal of it in the same breath.
**Effect on the audience:** They join in. By item two they are quietly predicting item three, which means you now own a second of their attention and can spend it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Lists, rants, rules, promises, inventories, character introductions. The craft rule is that items one and two must be genuinely parallel — same length, same register, same grammatical shape — because the break only reads as a break against a clean line. Make item three longer and more specific than the others; comic weight sits at the end.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, sketch, prose, monologue, voiceover, ad copy | genres: comedy, satire, kids, dramedy
**Avoid when:** You have already used it in the last two minutes. The triple is so reliable it becomes a tell: two close together and the audience hears the machine, starts predicting item three correctly, and the surprise is gone. One per scene, one per minute of stand-up, never two in a row.
**Example:**
> The retreat promised three things: silence, simplicity, and a man named Gordon who would take our phones and would not, under any circumstances, give them back.

**Yields to:** `comedy.topper` — where you have already used a triple in the last two minutes. Two close together and the audience hears the machine and predicts item three correctly.  
`comedy.rule_of_three`

---

### The Topper

**Also called:** the tag, the second laugh, the button on the button
**What it is:** A second punchline delivered immediately after the first, riding the same setup without rebuilding it. The audience is still laughing when it lands.
**Effect on the audience:** The laugh doubles instead of restarting. It also reads as generosity — the writer had more than they needed.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anywhere the first punchline got a real laugh and the premise still has fuel. The craft rule is that a topper must not require any new information. If you have to explain anything to land it, it is a new joke and it will drown in the wash of the first laugh. The best toppers are shorter than the punchline they follow.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, sketch, sitcom, dialogue scenes, short-form video | genres: comedy, dramedy, satire
**Avoid when:** The first punchline was a scene-ender. A topper on an exit line keeps the character in the room past their welcome and flattens the out. Also avoid stacking three toppers: by the third, the audience is watching you work.
**Example:**
> ORHAN: My father gave me exactly one piece of advice in his life. Never trust a man who irons his jeans.
> LEYLA: That's it?
> ORHAN: That's it. He died owing eleven thousand to a man who irons his jeans.

**Yields to:** `comedy.exit_joke` — where the first punchline was a scene-ender. A topper on an exit line keeps the character in the room past their welcome and flattens the out.  
`comedy.topper`

---

### Misdirection and the Reveal

**Also called:** the garden path, bait and switch, the pivot
**What it is:** The writer describes something in language that fits two situations, lets the audience assemble the wrong one, then supplies the detail that snaps everything into the other.
**Effect on the audience:** Retroactive rereading. They replay the setup and find it was honest the whole time, which is the specific pleasure — not being tricked, being outmanoeuvred fairly.
**Used for and where it works best:** Tops of bits, tops of sketches, prose paragraphs, anywhere you can afford three sentences of tone before the turn. The craft rule: the misdirection must never contain a lie. Everything before the reveal has to be literally true or the audience feels cheated rather than beaten. Build the false reading out of emotional register, not false facts.
**Best in:** formats: prose, stand-up, sketch, short-form video, voiceover | genres: comedy, satire, dark comedy, dramedy
**Avoid when:** The false reading is more interesting than the true one — you will get a groan, not a laugh. Also avoid it in dialogue where a character would obviously have said the clarifying detail first; the audience notices the withholding and it reads as authorial.
**Example:**
> The hospital called at four in the morning. They said my father had been asking for me all night, that it was urgent, that I should come at once.
>
> I drove ninety minutes in the rain.
>
> He wanted his charger.

**Yields to:** `comedy.one_misunderstanding` — The double reading has to live in dialogue.  
`comedy.misdirection`

---

### The Funny Word Goes Last

**Also called:** end-weighting, terminal placement, the back of the sentence
**What it is:** The single most absurd or concrete word in a joke is the final word before the laugh. Everything else is arranged to clear a path to it.
**Effect on the audience:** The laugh has somewhere to start. If the funny word sits mid-sentence the audience holds the laugh until you stop talking, and a held laugh is a smaller laugh.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every punchline, tag and gag caption. The craft rule is mechanical: find the word carrying the incongruity, then rewrite the sentence backwards from it. Subordinate clauses go to the front however ugly that looks on the page — spoken comedy does not obey written elegance.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, voiceover, sketch, dialogue, Carousel, short-form video | genres: comedy, kids, satire, ads
**Avoid when:** The line is doing character work rather than joke work and the natural word order tells us more about the speaker than the laugh is worth. A character who always front-loads the punchline is a character; a writer who does it is an amateur.
**Example:**
> Before: "A goat was, unbelievably, standing on the kitchen table eating the birthday cake when we got home."
>
> After: "We got home and there it was, on the kitchen table, eating the birthday cake — a goat."

**Yields to:** `voice.sentence_rhythm` — The line is doing character work, not joke work.  
`comedy.funny_word_last`

---

### The Literal Answer

**Also called:** taking it straight, the pedantic reply, the wilful misread
**What it is:** A character answers the words of a question instead of its intent, honestly and without malice, exposing how much of normal speech is padding.
**Effect on the audience:** Recognition plus superiority. They see the gap between what was asked and what was meant, and the character does not — or pretends not to.
**Used for and where it works best:** Two-handers, interrogations, interviews, doctors and officials — anywhere institutional language collides with a person. Works hand in glove with `dial.talking_past` and `char.status_transaction`. The craft rule: the literal answer must be shorter than the question. Length turns pedantry into a bit, and a bit invites the audience to notice the writer.
**Best in:** formats: sketch, sitcom, dialogue scenes, kids animation, short-form video | genres: comedy, absurdist, kids, dramedy
**Avoid when:** The character is meant to stay sympathetic and the question came from someone vulnerable. Literalism reads as cruelty the moment the asker is fragile.
**Example:**
> DOCTOR: Do you drink?
> MARWAN: Yes.
> DOCTOR: How much?
> MARWAN: All of it.

**Yields to:** `comedy.technically_correct` — The misread is a weapon, not innocence.  
`comedy.literal_answer`

---

### Understatement

**Also called:** litotes, the deadpan, the low setting
**What it is:** The response is calibrated far below the size of the event, and the gap between them is the joke. Nobody says the disaster is a disaster.
**Effect on the audience:** They supply the missing reaction themselves, which is why understatement lands harder than the scream would have. The audience does the work and takes the credit.
**Used for and where it works best:** Catastrophe, grief, humiliation — anything already loud. The craft rule: the event must be fully dramatised before the small line arrives. Understatement is a response, not a description; you cannot understate something the audience has not already seen at full size.
**Best in:** formats: prose, sitcom, film dialogue, sketch, documentary VO | genres: dark comedy, dramedy, satire, war comedy
**Avoid when:** The audience does not yet know how bad it is. Understating an offscreen event just reads as a character being vague, and the joke evaporates.
**Example:**
> The tent went down at two in the morning. The river came in at three. By dawn my brother had announced, out loud, in front of everyone including her parents, that the marriage was finished.
>
> Dad zipped his coat to the chin and looked at the sky.
>
> "Well," he said. "That's camping."

**Yields to:** `comedy.overstatement` — where the audience does not yet know how bad it is. Understating an offscreen event reads as a character being vague, and the joke evaporates.  
`comedy.understatement`

---

### Overstatement

**Also called:** hyperbole, comic exaggeration, the escalating claim
**What it is:** A true observation pushed past the point of possibility, in the same flat voice used for the true part, so the audience cannot find the exact sentence where it stopped being fact.
**Effect on the audience:** Delight at the commitment. The laugh comes not from the size of the exaggeration but from the refusal to acknowledge it as one.
**Used for and where it works best:** Character portraits, rants, the description of a relative or an institution. The craft rule: start inside the truth, and leave one small verifiable detail on the far side of the absurd claim. The detail is what sells it — a date, a sum of money, a place name.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, prose, sketch, kids animation, voiceover | genres: comedy, satire, kids, tall tale
**Avoid when:** You also need the audience to believe this character on a plot point. A narrator who exaggerates for laughs cannot then be trusted for the reveal without a deliberate reset.
**Example:**
> My uncle has not been wrong once since 1987. He has been contradicted. He has been sued. He has been asked to leave a funeral. But wrong, never.

**Yields to:** `comedy.understatement` — where you also need the audience to believe this character on a plot point. A narrator who exaggerates for laughs cannot then be trusted for the reveal without a deliberate reset.  
`comedy.overstatement`

---

### The Non Sequitur

**Also called:** the swerve, the disconnected reply, absurdist drift
**What it is:** A line that does not follow from the previous line and does not pretend to. The comedy is in the collision of two conversations sharing one room.
**Effect on the audience:** Destabilisation, then a specific joy — the sense that a character has a private interior logic and we are seeing only the exhaust of it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Marriages, long partnerships, bureaucracies — anywhere two people have stopped listening. The craft rule: the non sequitur must be consistent with the character's obsessions even while inconsistent with the scene. A random line is noise; a line that is the fourth visible symptom of one buried preoccupation is comedy. Related to `dial.deflection`, but deflection dodges on purpose and this does not.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, sketch, stage play, prose, kids animation | genres: absurdist, comedy, dramedy, surreal
**Avoid when:** The scene is carrying plot. Non sequiturs stop information transfer dead, and an audience that needs a fact will resent the swerve — put them in scenes where nothing must be learned.
**Example:**
> WIFE: We need to talk about money.
> HUSBAND: I've been thinking about owls.
> WIFE: We have four hundred until Thursday.
> HUSBAND: They can turn their heads the whole way round. Nobody knows why they're allowed.

**Yields to:** `comedy.funny_word_last` — where the scene is carrying plot. A non sequitur stops information transfer dead; a line that lands its own last word carries the fact and the laugh together.  
`comedy.non_sequitur`

---

### Funny Because True

**Also called:** observational comedy, recognition humour, the shared secret
**What it is:** Naming a behaviour everybody performs and nobody has said aloud. There is often no punchline at all — the act of accurate naming is the joke.
**Effect on the audience:** Relief and belonging. They laugh at having been seen, and at discovering that the thing they thought was their private stupidity is universal.
**Used for and where it works best:** Opening a set, opening a video, establishing a narrator's authority, any comedy that wants affection rather than superiority. The craft rule is granularity: the observation must be one level more specific than the audience expects. "Family photos are chaos" is nothing. The person still being called from the car is everything.
**Best in:** formats: stand-up, essay, short-form video, sitcom, voiceover | genres: observational comedy, dramedy, kids, ads
**Avoid when:** The observation is about a life you have not lived. Second-hand observational comedy reads instantly as research, and the response is not laughter but correction.
**Example:**
> Nobody has ever completed a family photograph. Someone is always still being called from the car. And the photo you actually keep, the one that ends up in the frame, is always the one where four people are looking at the person still being called from the car.

`comedy.observational_truth`

## Section 2 — Timing on the Page

### Comic Timing Written, Not Performed

**Also called:** the beat, the pause on the page, rhythm control
**What it is:** Timing is not a performance decision you leave to an actor. It is built with line length, paragraph breaks, stage directions, sentence rhythm and where a page turn falls.
**Effect on the audience:** They feel the silence before the punchline as a held breath rather than as dead air, because the layout told them to hold it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Every written joke that will be spoken or read. Concretely: a punchline gets its own line; a beat is written as an action, never as the word "beat" four times; a long line before a short line makes the short line faster; and a question repeated with no answer between is the cheapest silence in the trade. In prose, the paragraph break is the pause.
**Best in:** formats: screenplay, sketch, stage, prose, comics, storyboards | genres: all comedy
**Avoid when:** You are writing for an improviser or a comic performer with their own rhythm, where over-notated pauses fight the performance. Give the structure, not the metronome.
**Example:**
> Before: "After a long pause, she admitted that she had in fact already told everyone."
>
> After:
> "Did you tell them?"
> She looked at the ceiling.
> "Did you tell them?"
> "I told them in March."

**Yields to:** `comedy.game_of_the_scene` — where you are writing for an improviser or a comic performer with their own rhythm. Give them the structure, not the metronome.  
`comedy.timing_on_the_page`

## Section 3 — The Engines

### Status as the Engine

**Also called:** Johnstone status, the see-saw, playing high and low
**What it is:** Keith Johnstone's observation that every exchange is a status transaction, and that most comedy is the see-saw of one person raising themselves while lowering another — or lowering themselves to gain something. Jokes are the visible sparks; status is the motor underneath.
**Effect on the audience:** They track an invisible scoreboard nobody told them about, and they laugh at the moment it tips. This is why a scene can be funny with no joke in it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any two-hander with nothing happening. When a comic scene is dead, the diagnosis is almost always that both characters are playing the same status and neither is moving. The craft rule: give each character a status they are playing and a status they actually hold, and make the gap visible to us and invisible to them. Then engineer a `char.status_flip` at the value turn — see `scene.value_turn` and `char.status_transaction`.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, stage, sketch, film dialogue, prose | genres: comedy of manners, farce, workplace comedy, satire, drama
**Avoid when:** Never avoid it — but never narrate it. The moment a character says "you think you're better than me," the machinery is on the outside of the scene and it stops working.
**Example:**
> Two neighbours. One broken fence.
>
> "I've had a man look at it."
> "A man."
> "A professional."
> "Is he the same professional who did your drive?"
>
> A long pause.
>
> "He's a different professional."

`comedy.status_engine`

---

### The Straight Man

**Also called:** the feed, the audience surrogate, the anchor
**What it is:** A character who reacts to the absurdity at normal human scale and in doing so tells the audience how big the absurdity is. Without a fixed point there is no measurable distortion.
**Effect on the audience:** Orientation. They know where to stand. A scene where everyone is wacky is not twice as funny, it is unwatchable, because nothing is deviating from anything.
**Used for and where it works best:** Duos, workplace ensembles, any world with one madman in it. The craft rule: the straight man must want something in the scene, not merely disapprove of the comic. Disapproval is a stance, not a tactic — the moment their reaction becomes a strategy to get something, the scene has an engine (see `scene.tactic_change`). They should also take roughly one laugh in four, or the audience stops caring about the person they are watching through.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, sketch, feature film, stage, kids animation | genres: comedy, farce, workplace comedy, dramedy, kids, buddy
**Avoid when:** The comic character is already self-aware. Two self-aware characters produce commentary, not comedy. And avoid a straight man who is only competent — competence with no flaw of its own becomes a lecturer.
**Example:**
> FADI: I've bought a horse.
> SAM: You live on the fourth floor.
> FADI: It's not a big horse.
> SAM: Which floor is the horse on, Fadi.

**Yields to:** `comedy.generative_pairing` — where the comic character is already self-aware. Two self-aware characters produce commentary rather than comedy, so the friction has to come from the pairing's structure instead.  
`comedy.straight_man`

---

### The Wrong-Sized Reaction

**Also called:** miscalibration, the broken emotional thermostat, inappropriate affect
**What it is:** A character whose emotional response is reliably the wrong size for the event — catastrophic about small things, serene about disasters. The character is consistent; it is reality that keeps changing scale around them.
**Effect on the audience:** Constant low-grade delight, with total predictability of flavour and none of content. They know how this character will be wrong, never what they will say.
**Used for and where it works best:** Ensembles that need one reliable generator. The craft rule: pick the direction and never switch it. A character who under-reacts to death and over-reacts to parking is funny; one who over-reacts to everything is just loud. Pair it with `char.load_bearing_contradiction` so the miscalibration means something.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, film, prose, sketch, kids animation | genres: comedy, dark comedy, dramedy, absurdist
**Avoid when:** The story needs this character to carry the emotional climax. A miscalibrated character cannot deliver a straight emotional beat without spending their whole comic credit — which can be a magnificent move, but it is a one-time payment.
**Example:**
> The plane dropped. The lockers opened, somebody screamed the name of a god, a man two rows up began loudly confessing things to his wife.
>
> Beside me, my aunt put down her crossword, looked out of the window and said, "Well — at least we'll get there early."

**Yields to:** `comedy.deliberate_stop` — This character must carry the emotional climax.  
`comedy.wrong_reaction`

---

### Comic Character Construction

**Also called:** the one lie, the fixed delusion, the engine character
**What it is:** A comic character is built on a single false claim they make about themselves and cannot stop making, plus a world that keeps disproving it. Every line they speak is either defending the lie or being caught by it.
**Effect on the audience:** They laugh before the character speaks, because they can see the collision coming and the character cannot. It is `info.dramatic_irony` shrunk to fit one person.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any character who must stay funny across a series rather than one scene. The craft rule: write the lie as a first-person sentence — "I am not a jealous person," "I am owed more than this," "I am the only adult here" — and then build every scene by putting that sentence under pressure. Give them an `char.incompetence_zone` adjacent to the lie, not identical to it.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, series, film, prose, kids animation | genres: comedy, satire, dramedy, kids, farce
**Avoid when:** The story asks this character to genuinely change. The lie is the engine; dismantle it and they stop generating. If they must change, that is the series finale, not episode four.
**Example:**
> "I'm not a jealous person."
> "You followed the postman."
> "I walked in the same direction as the postman. For forty minutes. Because I am not a jealous person and I don't have to prove that to anybody."

**Yields to:** `comedy.comic_ending` — where the story asks this character to genuinely change. The lie is the engine: dismantle it and they stop generating, so if they must change that is the finale, not episode four.  
`comedy.comic_character_engine`

## Section 4 — Escalation and the Long Joke

### Escalation and the Comic Spiral

**Also called:** the build, the snowball, raising the stakes comically
**What it is:** Each attempt to fix the problem creates a larger problem of the same kind, so the situation inflates without ever changing subject. The spiral is the difference between a sketch and a story.
**Effect on the audience:** Mounting anticipatory dread that is indistinguishable from mounting pleasure. They start predicting the next escalation and enjoy being outbid.
**Used for and where it works best:** Half-hour comedy, farce, short-form video, any comic set piece longer than thirty seconds. The craft rule: every escalation must be caused by the protagonist's own choice, never by coincidence. A run of bad luck is not escalation, it is weather. Escalate in kind, too — if the first problem is a lie, the fifth must still be a lie, only structurally enormous. Around beat four, use `scene.third_party_arrival` to compress the clock.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, film, sketch, short-form video, prose | genres: farce, comedy, crime comedy, dramedy
**Avoid when:** You have no ending. An escalation with no terminal beat becomes a shaggy dog, and an audience forgives that about once per career. Know the final beat before you write beat one.
**Example:**
> 1. He tells his wife the car is at the garage.
> 2. The car is not at the garage. It is at his brother's.
> 3. His brother has sold it.
> 4. His brother has sold it to the neighbour.
> 5. The neighbour is driving them both to the airport on Friday.

`comedy.escalation_spiral`

---

### The Running Gag

**Also called:** the recurring bit, the motif joke, the series gag
**What it is:** One element — a phrase, an object, an entrance — returns at intervals, each return altered by everything that has happened since. The gag barely changes; its meaning does.
**Effect on the audience:** Ownership. By the third appearance they feel like insiders, and part of the laugh is at their own memory working.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anything longer than five minutes, especially series an audience returns to weekly. The craft rules: three to five appearances is the working range; each should be shorter than the last; and the final one should either escalate to the logical extreme or land in a context that inverts it. Retire it one appearance before you want to. Distinct from `dial.callback_line`, which is a single verbal echo.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, series, film, sketch show, prose, kids animation | genres: comedy, farce, kids, satire, dramedy
**Avoid when:** The gag has no variation available. A gag that can only repeat identically is a catchphrase, and catchphrases are audience management, not comedy — see `comedy.repetition_turn` for why the fourth identical repeat kills it. Kids' content is the exception: small children request the same gag on purpose, and there the identical repeat is an asset (`comedy.kids_comedy`).
**Example:**
> Act 1, to his wife, on the phone: "The cat is fine."
>
> Act 2, through a locked bathroom door, to nobody: "The cat is fine."
>
> Act 3, at the funeral, to an elderly woman he has never met in his life: "The cat is fine."
>
> She nods as if this settles something.

**Yields to:** `comedy.repetition_turn` — where the gag has no variation available. A gag that can only repeat identically is a catchphrase, which is audience management rather than comedy.  
`comedy.running_gag`

---

### The Callback Payoff

**Also called:** the long fuse, the delayed detonation, the planted joke
**What it is:** A detail planted early with no comic weight returns much later in a context that converts it. The first mention is not a joke; the second is, and it is far bigger than either mention deserves.
**Effect on the audience:** The best laugh available in long-form comedy, because the audience gets to feel clever and the writer gets to feel structural. It also retroactively promises that everything else was deliberate too.
**Used for and where it works best:** Endings. The last five minutes of a film, the closer of a set, the final line of a chapter. The craft rule: plant it as information, not as a gag. If the plant got a laugh, the payoff is a repeat; if the plant got nothing, the payoff gets everything. Distance is the multiplier — see `end.callback` for the structural version.
**Best in:** formats: film, stand-up set, series, novel, sketch show, short-form video | genres: comedy, dramedy, farce, satire
**Avoid when:** The audience has to remember two things at once to get it. A callback that requires reconstruction is a puzzle, and puzzles do not make people laugh, they make people nod.
**Example:**
> Early, at a wedding: "My father's entire philosophy was this. Never trust a man who irons his jeans."
>
> Ninety minutes later, in a solicitor's office, her husband's lawyer slides the divorce papers across the desk and offers her a pen. She looks down at his knees.
>
> "Nice crease," she says.

**Yields to:** `comedy.short_form_shape` — where the audience would have to remember two things at once. A callback that requires reconstruction is a puzzle, and puzzles make people nod rather than laugh.  
`comedy.callback_payoff`

---

### Repetition and the Point Where It Turns

**Also called:** diminishing returns, the third-time problem, comic fatigue
**What it is:** Repeating a comic beat gets funnier, then stops, then gets funny again on the far side if you push much further — but the flat middle is real and most writers die in it.
**Effect on the audience:** First time surprise, second recognition, third anticipation, fourth impatience, tenth a new and different laugh at your refusal to stop. The curve is a U and the bottom of it is deadly.
**Used for and where it works best:** Comedy that can afford to risk the middle — absurdist work, animation, live theatre where you can feel the room. The craft rule: stop at three or commit past seven, but never stop at four or five. That count is for a beat repeated unchanged; a gag that returns at intervals, altered each time, is `comedy.running_gag` and keeps its own working range. The strongest version breaks the pattern by withholding: the audience has been trained to expect the knock, so the biggest laugh is the silence where the knock should be.
**Best in:** formats: animation, sketch, stage, prose, kids content, short-form video | genres: absurdist, kids, farce, comedy
**Avoid when:** You cannot feel the audience and cannot cut — a locked-picture ad, a subtitled export, a sponsored short. The long repetition is a high-variance play; do not make it where you have no way to bail out.
**Example:**
> The neighbour knocks. Funny.
> The neighbour knocks again. Funnier.
> The neighbour knocks a third time. Not funny — now they are just waiting.
>
> Nobody knocks.
>
> The whole family turns and stares at the door.

**Yields to:** `comedy.running_gag` — where you cannot feel the audience and cannot cut: a locked-picture ad, a subtitled export, a sponsored short. The long repetition is a high-variance play and this is not the place to make it.  
`comedy.repetition_turn`

## Section 5 — The Comic Modes

### The Farce Engine

**Also called:** the door play, high-speed comedy, the machine of lies
**What it is:** A structure in which one lie must be maintained in a confined space against a hard deadline, while the number of people who must be kept apart keeps rising. Farce is not a tone, it is a machine with a clock in it.
**Effect on the audience:** Physical tension released as laughter. They are doing arithmetic — who knows what, who is behind which door — and the laugh is the arithmetic resolving badly.
**Used for and where it works best:** Confined settings with multiple exits: a flat, a hotel, an office, a wedding. The rules are strict — one lie, not several; a real deadline stated out loud early; and every character needs an urgent reason to be in the room, because a farce dies the second someone could reasonably leave. Escalate with `comedy.escalation_spiral` and detonate at a `scene.public_scene`.
**Best in:** formats: stage, film, sitcom, short-form video | genres: farce, comedy, romantic comedy, crime comedy
**Avoid when:** Your characters can text. Modern farce has to disable communication plausibly in the first two minutes or the structure becomes a question the audience keeps asking. Also avoid farce when you want the audience to feel for anyone — farce burns sympathy as fuel.
**Example:**
> "He's in the bathroom."
> "Who is?"
> "Nobody's in the bathroom."
> "Then why is it locked?"
> "It's always locked. It's a very private bathroom."

**Yields to:** `comedy.tragedy_in_comedy` — where you want the audience to feel for anyone. Farce burns sympathy as fuel, and the two cannot run in the same sequence.  
`comedy.farce_engine`

---

### Comedy of Manners

**Also called:** drawing-room comedy, social comedy, comedy of etiquette
**What it is:** Comedy generated by the gap between what a social code requires people to say and what they actually mean. Nothing physical happens; everything happens in the choice of words.
**Effect on the audience:** The pleasure of decoding. They hear both the sentence and its translation, and the laugh is the distance between them.
**Used for and where it works best:** Any society with a rigid code — class, religion, diaspora family, corporate HR, academia. The craft rule: show the code working correctly at least once before you show it failing, or the audience cannot hear the deviation. Write the politest possible sentence that also lands a blow — see `dial.concession_that_wins`.
**Best in:** formats: stage, film, novel, sitcom, series | genres: comedy of manners, satire, romantic comedy, literary fiction
**Avoid when:** Your audience does not share the code. Manners comedy is the most culture-locked form there is; a joke about the correct number of times to refuse tea is invisible to anyone who has never had to refuse tea. See `comedy.translation_resistance`.
**Example:**
> "You must come for dinner."
> "We'd love to."
> "Shall we say a date?"
> "Let's not spoil it."

**Yields to:** `comedy.translation_resistance` — where your audience does not share the code. Manners comedy is the most culture-locked form there is: a joke about the correct number of times to refuse tea is invisible to anyone who has never had to refuse tea.  
`comedy.comedy_of_manners`

---

### Satire With a Target

**Also called:** the critique joke, institutional comedy, ridicule with an address
**What it is:** Comedy aimed at a specific person, institution or habit, built so the laugh is also an argument. Without a target it is not satire, it is just tone.
**Effect on the audience:** Complicity in a judgement. They laugh, and in laughing they have agreed with something — which is why satire is the most persuasive comic mode and the most resented.
**Used for and where it works best:** When the target has power and the audience already suspects what you are about to prove. The craft rule: satirise the mechanism, not the people caught in it. Mock the ministry, not the man queuing at it — the moment the target is the weaker party the form inverts into bullying and the room goes cold. Push the institution's own logic until it indicts itself, rather than adding an authorial opinion on top.
**Best in:** formats: sketch, essay, series, novel, short-form video, animation | genres: satire, political comedy, dark comedy, dystopian
**Avoid when:** You are unwilling to be specific. Vague satire aimed at "the system" reads as cowardice, and it dates faster than named satire because there is nothing in it to check against.
**Example:**
> In response to the ongoing water shortage, the Ministry has today renamed itself the Ministry of Water Abundance.
>
> A spokesman confirmed that the taps remain dry, but that the signage has been fully upgraded and the ribbon-cutting was, by all accounts, well attended.

`comedy.satire_target`

---

### Cringe and Social Comedy

**Also called:** comedy of embarrassment, the awkward, second-hand shame
**What it is:** The audience watches a person violate a social rule they have not noticed they are violating, and is given no escape from the scene.
**Effect on the audience:** Physical discomfort that resolves as laughter — or does not, which is the risk. It is the only comic mode whose success looks like the audience covering their eyes.
**Used for and where it works best:** Mockumentary, workplace comedy, weddings and funerals. The rules: the cringing character must be trying to be liked, not trying to be cruel; there must be one witness in frame doing nothing; and the scene must run about four beats past comfortable, because the discomfort is the product. Use `tens.release_valve` sparingly here — releasing the tension is exactly what most writers wrongly do.
**Best in:** formats: sitcom, film, short-form video, stage | genres: cringe comedy, workplace comedy, dark comedy, dramedy
**Avoid when:** The character has no dignity left to lose. Cringe requires an intact self-image to puncture; a character already humiliated generates pity, and pity is not funny at any length.
**Example:**
> He raises his glass. "I've known the bride since she was — well. Since she was with Karim."
>
> Nobody drinks. He carries on.
>
> "Which is its own story. And a lesson for us all, frankly. Anyway. To the happy couple. And to Karim. Wherever he is."

**Yields to:** `emo.humiliation_comedy` — where the character has no dignity left to lose. Cringe needs an intact self-image to puncture; a character already humiliated generates pity, and pity is not funny at any length.  
`comedy.cringe`

---

### Dark Comedy and Its Rules

**Also called:** black comedy, gallows humour, the taboo joke
**What it is:** Comedy built on death, illness, violence or disgrace, which works by keeping the tone flat while the content is enormous. The laugh is a pressure valve on a real fear.
**Effect on the audience:** Permission. They have been carrying dread about this subject and you have given them a legal way to put it down for four seconds.
**Used for and where it works best:** Grief, war, hospitals, the bureaucracy of the dead. The rules are the ones people ignore: the joke must side with the powerless, never with the harm; the horror must be treated as fully real elsewhere in the piece; and the comic voice must belong to someone inside the situation, never to a narrator standing outside enjoying it. Dark comedy from a safe distance is not dark comedy, it is a smirk.
**Best in:** formats: film, novel, sitcom, stand-up, stage | genres: dark comedy, war comedy, crime comedy, dramedy, satire
**Avoid when:** The audience is currently inside the event. A joke about a disaster is a gift to survivors ten years later and an assault on them in week one. Timing here is measured in years, not beats.
**Example:**
> "Dad's ashes are in the boot."
> "Which boot?"
> "The car boot."
> "So he's coming to the wedding."
> "He's parked at the wedding. There's a difference."

**Yields to:** `comedy.joke_shelf_life` — where the audience is currently inside the event. A joke about a disaster is a gift to survivors ten years later and an assault on them in week one; timing here is measured in years.  
`comedy.dark_comedy`

---

### Physical Comedy Written for the Page

**Also called:** slapstick on paper, the visual gag, action-line comedy
**What it is:** A physical joke specified precisely enough in the writing that it exists before anyone performs it — written as geometry and consequence rather than as "comically."
**Effect on the audience:** The most universal laugh available, and the one least dependent on language, culture or attention.
**Used for and where it works best:** Animation, kids content, short-form video, silent openings, and anything that will be exported to other languages. The craft rule: never write that something is funny, write the physics. The word "comically" in an action line is an admission that the gag has not been designed. Specify the object, the space it cannot fit through, and the second attempt — the second attempt is where the laugh is.
**Best in:** formats: animation, film, short-form video, kids content, storyboards | genres: kids, slapstick, farce, comedy, ads
**Avoid when:** The budget, the performer or the model cannot execute it. A physical gag that half-works is worse than none — the audience sees the intention and the failure at the same time. Design the gag to the tool you actually have.
**Example:**
> Before: "He comically struggles to get the ladder into the room."
>
> After: "He carries the ladder in horizontally. Everyone in the room ducks. He turns to apologise. Everyone ducks again."

`comedy.physical_on_page`

---

## Section 6 — Comedy Across Formats and Languages

### Short-Form Comic Shape

**Also called:** the vertical joke, the two-second hook, the scroll-proof bit
**What it is:** A comic structure compressed so the hook lands in the first two seconds, the escalation takes the middle, and the payoff arrives before attention breaks — roughly a tenth hook, three-quarters build, a fifth payoff.
**Effect on the audience:** They do not scroll. That is the entire measurable effect and the only one the format rewards.
**Used for and where it works best:** Reels, Shorts, TikTok, pre-roll. The rules: write the last line first and build backwards; the hook does not have to make sense yet, only create a question; and the payoff must be confirmed visually — a reaction shot or a final image — because a large share of the audience is watching muted. Cut the setup to one sentence; there is no room for two.
**Best in:** formats: short-form video, Reels, Shorts, TikTok, ads, kids shorts | genres: comedy, observational, kids, satire, sketch
**Avoid when:** The joke needs a slow burn or a relationship the audience has not got yet. Short-form cannot afford `comedy.callback_payoff` inside a single video — but it can run one across a series, which is the format's real long game.
**Example:**
> 0:00 — He turns the camera to himself, whispering. "Do not, under any circumstances, let my mother near the microphone."
> 0:02 — Mother. Microphone.
> 0:07 — "—and that is why he is not allowed back into Lebanon."
> 0:09 — Cut to him, phone down, walking fully clothed into the sea.

**Yields to:** `comedy.callback_payoff` — where the joke needs a slow burn or a relationship the audience has not got yet. Short form cannot afford one inside a single video, but it can run one across a series, which is the format's real long game.  
`comedy.short_form_shape`

---

### Comedy in Kids' Content

**Also called:** children's humour, animation gag writing, family comedy
**What it is:** Comedy built on surprise, exaggeration, repetition and the pleasure of a child knowing more than an adult on screen — not on irony, which is the last comic faculty to develop.
**Effect on the audience:** For the child, mastery: they got the joke, so they understand the world. For the adult in the room, a second layer that keeps them watching without ever making them the target.
**Used for and where it works best:** Songs, animation, picture books, kids shorts. The rules: brevity above everything, because the attention window is real; build the comedy into who the character is rather than what they say, since young audiences read behaviour long before wordplay; put the child character one step ahead of the adult; and treat requested identical repetition as comfort and participation. When the repeated beat must keep producing new laughs, vary or escalate its meaning under `comedy.running_gag`.
**Best in:** formats: animation, kids songs, picture book, kids shorts, preschool | genres: kids, family, educational, musical
**Avoid when:** You are writing over the child's head to the parent. A joke aimed entirely at the adult is a betrayal of the primary audience, and children detect condescension faster than adults detect anything.
**Example:**
> "I have eaten your homework," said the dog.
> "You can TALK?"
> "Yes. And I have eaten your homework."
> "But you can TALK."
> "I can see we are not going to get past the homework."

**Yields to:** `sub.dual_audience` — wherever you are writing over the child's head to the parent. A joke aimed entirely at the adult is a betrayal of the primary audience; a second layer is a different design and has to be built as one.  
`comedy.kids_comedy`

---

### Building a Joke That Survives Translation

**Also called:** transcreation-proofing, portable comedy, the exportable gag
**What it is:** Designing comedy so its mechanism lives in situation, behaviour or image rather than in the sound or double meaning of specific words — because a pun has no equivalent in the next language and a local reference has no equivalent anywhere.
**Effect on the audience:** In the source language, the same laugh as any other joke. In the target language, still a laugh — not a small achievement, since the ordinary outcome is silence.
**Used for and where it works best:** Anything that will be subtitled, dubbed or exported. The rules: put the load on what a character does, not on what a word sounds like; avoid punchlines that are proper nouns the audience must recognise; and where you must use wordplay, mark it in the script as a transcreation point so the translator writes a new joke in that slot instead of translating yours into a corpse. Subtitle length is a hard constraint too — a joke needing more than two lines on screen gets cut for length before anyone judges its quality.
**Best in:** formats: animation, film, kids content, short-form video, ads, documentary | genres: kids, family, comedy, satire
**Avoid when:** You are writing for one language and one place and you know it. Portability costs specificity, and specificity is where most of the best comedy lives — do not export-proof a joke nobody is going to export.
**Example:**
> Survives: a man carries a ladder horizontally through a crowded wedding and the entire top table ducks in sequence.
>
> Does not survive: "I told my wife she should embrace her mistakes. She gave me a hug."

**Yields to:** `comedy.comedy_of_manners` — where you are writing for one language and one place and you know it. Portability costs specificity, and specificity is where most of the best comedy lives.  
`comedy.translation_resistance`

---

## Section 7 — Failure Modes

### The Joke That Stops the Story

**Also called:** the joke tax, the dead-air gag, the scene that pauses to be funny
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A joke that requires the scene to hold still while it happens. The characters stop pursuing what they want, a bit occurs, and the scene restarts from exactly where it was with nothing changed.
**Effect on the audience:** The laugh lands and the story loses altitude. Worse, they learn that this piece will pause for jokes, and they stop believing the stakes.
**Used for and where it works best:** How to spot it in your own draft: delete the joke and check whether anything downstream changes. If nothing does, it was a tax, not a scene. The repair is not to cut the line but to make it a tactic — a joke is safe when a character is using it to get something.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. The most common carrier is the "funny friend" scene and the tension-breaking quip during action; `tens.comic_relief_as_tension` is the version that does the job properly, because there the joke raises pressure instead of venting it.
**Example:**
> Before:
> The door is kicked in.
> RASHID: You know what the worst thing about this country is? Parking.
>
> After:
> The door is kicked in.
> RASHID (fast, to his wife): If they ask, I'm your brother.
> WIFE: You look nothing like my brother.
> RASHID: I'll say I take after the mother.

**Yields to:** `tens.comic_relief_as_tension` — always. The common carriers are the "funny friend" scene and the tension-breaking quip during action; the other card does the job properly, because there the joke raises pressure instead of venting it.  
`comedy.joke_that_stops_story`

---

### The Character Who Is Only Funny

**Also called:** the joke machine, the gag dispenser, the character with no want
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A character who exists to produce jokes and has no objective in any scene. They enter, deliver, and leave the plot exactly where they found it.
**Effect on the audience:** Diminishing returns, which the writer mistakes for the audience tiring of comedy. In fact the audience has worked out that this person cannot affect anything, and attention follows consequence.
**Used for and where it works best:** Diagnose it by asking what this character loses if the scene goes badly. If the answer is nothing, they are furniture that talks. The repair is one line of work: give them something they want in this specific scene that the comedy is a tactic for getting.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. A `char.load_bearing_contradiction` converts a gag dispenser into a person in about a page, and costs none of the jokes.
**Example:**
> Before:
> MO enters. "Traffic! Am I right? Anyway — here's my impression of a fax machine."
> He does it. He leaves. The scene continues.
>
> After:
> MO enters needing two hundred by Thursday and does the fax machine, because the fax machine is the only thing that has ever worked on his sister, and they both know it, and she is already reaching for her bag before he finishes.

**Yields to:** `char.load_bearing_contradiction` — always. It converts a gag dispenser into a person in about a page and costs none of the jokes.  
`comedy.only_funny_character`

---

### The Punchline the Audience Reaches First

**Also called:** telegraphing, the visible gag, arriving second
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** The turn is predictable from the setup, so the audience assembles the joke before you deliver it and then has to sit through the delivery.
**Effect on the audience:** Not annoyance — worse, patience. They wait politely for you to catch up. The laugh is replaced by a small internal note that they are ahead of the writer, and once that note exists it never goes away.
**Used for and where it works best:** The test is brutal and reliable: read the setup to someone and stop. If they can say the punchline, it is dead. The repair is counter-intuitive — do not hide the obvious answer better, hand it over immediately and make the joke whatever is on the far side of it.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always. Whatever the audience guessed is now your setup; the real punchline has to arrive from a direction the pattern did not predict, which is `struct.kishotenketsu` operating at joke scale.
**Example:**
> Before:
> "What's in the box?"
> "Nothing."
> "It's moving."
> "It's not moving."
> "It's a duck, isn't it."
> "It's a duck."
>
> After:
> "There's a duck in the box."
> "I know there's a duck in the box. I'm asking why the box is in the oven."

**Yields to:** `struct.kishotenketsu` — always. Whatever the audience guessed is now your setup, and the real punchline has to arrive from a direction the pattern did not predict.  
`comedy.audience_gets_there_first`

---

### The Explained Joke

**Also called:** underlining, the laugh track in prose, the joke with a footnote
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** The writer lands a joke and then adds a clause telling the reader it was a joke, why it worked, or how the room reacted — most often a sentence starting "which was funny because."
**Effect on the audience:** The laugh is confiscated. Comedy requires the audience to make the final connection themselves; explaining it makes them a spectator at their own joke, and the result is mild embarrassment on the writer's behalf.
**Used for and where it works best:** The mechanical check: find the sentence immediately after each punchline and delete it. If the joke now fails, it never worked and the explanation was carrying it. The same defect appears in dialogue as a second character laughing on the audience's behalf.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** Always, with one exception: a character who explains their own jokes. Then the explanation is `comedy.cringe` and the explaining is the joke — but that is a character choice you commit to, not a habit you fall into.
**Example:**
> Before:
> "She's got a face like a dropped pie," he said, and grinned. It was a cruel thing to say, but funny, because her face really did have that collapsed quality.
>
> After:
> "She's got a face like a dropped pie," he said.
> Nobody laughed, which is how he knew it would be round the whole office by lunchtime.

**Yields to:** `comedy.cringe` — for the one exception: a character who explains their own jokes, where the explaining is the joke. That is a character choice you commit to, not a habit you fall into.  
`comedy.explained_joke`

---

## Coverage

Covered here: the joke unit (setup and punchline, rule of three, topper, misdirection, end-weighting, literal answer, understatement, overstatement, non sequitur, observational truth); comic timing on the page; the four engines (status, straight man, the miscalibrated reaction, comic character construction); escalation and the long joke (the spiral, the running gag, the callback payoff, the repetition curve); the modes (farce, manners, satire, cringe, dark comedy, physical comedy); format and language (short-form shape, kids comedy, translation resistance); and four named failures.

Not covered in this file (some are in [Part 2](cat-comedy-2.md); the rest are not yet written, and no further part is promised): the wordplay family (pun, paraprosdokian, malapropism, spoonerism, double entendre); the comic premise and the act-out; escalation by category shift; deadpan versus mugging; the comic rant and the comic monologue; irony types and sarcasm on the page; parody, pastiche and spoof; mockumentary grammar; the comic ensemble and the four-hander; the comic villain; the fool, the trickster and the clown lineage; anticlimax and bathos; comedy of scale and the miniature; absurdism and dream logic; comic names and naming; the unreliable comic narrator; the funny sentence at word level (rhythm, plosives, syllable count); insult architecture and the punch-up rule; self-deprecation and its status trap; comic songs and lyric jokes; the comic advert and brand-safe humour; improv principles that transfer to the page; the table read and how to test a joke; rewriting a joke that half-works; the alt and the alt-alt; joke density and pacing across an act; comedy inside horror and inside action; the romantic comedy engine; the workplace status grid; comedy with child performers; culture-specific comic forms and the diaspora joke; and the remaining failure modes — the mean joke that loses the room, the punch-down reversal, the reference that dates, the joke only the writer's friends get, tone drift across an episode, and the ending that jokes instead of landing.

*Build notes from when this file was drafted — targets, running totals and what remained to be written — are kept verbatim in the [coverage history](../tools/history/coverage-history.md). They were true of the draft, not of the file, so they no longer sit here as if they were measurements.*
